fatal_errors: The hypothesis addresses HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture testing, whereas the target concerns composition screening in the Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W system and room-temperature quasi-static compression of as-cast Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5.

It replaces the target intervention—validation of a rule-of-mixtures modulus model followed by screening 38,326 compositions using modulus, VEC, and density—with an unsubstantiated GNN-CALPHAD workflow.

It predicts toughness despite providing neither toughness training data nor a physically and statistically validated toughness model; the target paper did not predict or measure tensile fracture toughness.
The claimed 20% accuracy and 30% efficiency gains are unsupported by cited evidence, learning curves, dataset size, error definitions, uncertainty estimates, or computational-cost measurements.
The proposed benchmark is not genuinely blinded or prospective because HfNbTiVAl10 is included in the training dataset, creating leakage risk.
The falsification rule does not define the error metric, fixed comparator, train-test split, independent test compositions, specimen geometry, testing protocol, or confidence intervals.
explanation: The generated hypothesis is a generic, potentially plausible machine-learning proposal but does not reconstruct the hidden work. The target used a simple composition-based design strategy: modulus estimates were validated against roughly 130–132 HEAs, 38,326 Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W compositions were screened, and a low-VEC/high-modulus composition was selected. Its proposed mechanism was increased dislocation mobility from reduced VEC and a lower Peierls–Nabarro barrier, producing extensive slip and delayed cracking while retaining high strength. Experimentally, the designed alloy reached 35.7 ± 0.9% compressive fracture strain, 1115 ± 18 MPa yield strength, and 2550 ± 75 MPa compressive strength. None of these composition, mechanism, condition, or outcome details appears in the generated hypothesis. Its baseline and applicability boundary are stated only generally, and no prior evidence is supplied. The benchmark could become discriminating only with strict external holdout alloys, a preregistered comparator and error metric, standardized tensile/fracture protocols, uncertainty-aware acceptance thresholds, and no inclusion of benchmark materials in model development.
